text.en: Which state or Union Territory do you live in, and in which part of the country is it? Imagine travelling from the snowy north to the sandy west, the muddy delta in the east and the sea in the south. In this chapter, a girl called Shaana travels the length and breadth of India with her parents and writes postcards to her classmates.

You talk about a place you enjoyed travelling to, who you went with, how you travelled and what you learned. You write details about your own State or Union Territory: its part of the country (North, East, Northeast, West, South or Centre), capital, language, river or rivers, tourist attraction and food. You also recall the states with Pradesh in their names, say where each lies, and note a special feature of each.
Shaana lives on Rameswaram island and travels with her parents, writing to friends at school. On 30 April she is at the Thajiwas glacier in Kashmir, far in the north. The glaciers are white and blue, they wear four layers of clothes, and her parents throw snowballs at each other. On 10 May she is in Himachal Pradesh, which is very quiet, with many mountains to see from the train cabin. Colourful birds wake her with chirping at sunrise in the east. The growling she hears in the west at dusk is only her father snoring.
On 24 May she writes from the Sundarbans in West Bengal. She goes in a small boat and learns that such places are called wetlands, where mangrove trees grow even in seawater. Her mother is sad that the place floods so much today. They see crocodiles and a lonely snake. On 30 May she has travelled east to west, from West Bengal to Gujarat, in two and a half days. She finds herself in the desert, hot and dry, with sand everywhere, like a beach without a sea. She loves the pretty, colourful clothes. Her mother gives her a surprise test and she scores 88 per cent.
On 7 June she is at the Narmada river, which flows to the centre of India, reached by driving east from the desert in six hours. She goes rafting and finds the river wild and scary, and her father decides never to go rafting again. Appa says the river once had much more water. On 12 June, in Goa in the south-west, she sees plateaus, hills, beaches and many tunnels the train goes through. She used to be afraid of tunnels, but not any more, so her attitude changes from fear to comfort.
On 17 June they travel south, reach Chennai, and on the way to Puducherry they learn to surf. The beaches are rougher and the water browner than on her island. On 22 June she crosses the Pamban bridge, and sees the ocean on both sides. On 24 June they stop at Olaikaadu beach. There were no diving suits her size, so she floats and watches fish while her parents dive. On 25 June she writes to her parents, thanking them for the journey across forests, glaciers, deserts, wetlands, plateaus and mountains, with many languages and new people. The book is an excerpt from a book by C. G. Salamander, and the postcards teach us about the many landscapes, people and cultures of India.
When she says she never knew such a place existed, the feeling is wonder. Her mother is sad about the Sundarbans flooding because climate and sea changes cause frequent floods and damage the wetland. Slight nervousness shows in her wish that crocodiles and the snake would not follow her home. She stays awake in the train because she loves looking out of the window. Her wish to tour the plateaus with friends shows her sense of connection. The postcards are informal letters, with greetings and sign-offs such as Love, Shaana.
Directions give the position of places: north, south, east, west and combinations like south-west. Shaana uses them to tell where she is. Postcards and letters to friends are informal. They use greetings such as Dear class, short sentences and friendly closings such as Your best friend. Words in the text include chirping, a short, sharp sound made by birds; snoring, a loud noise made while sleeping; rafting, travelling down a river in a rubber boat; surf, to ride a wave on a board; dive, to swim underwater with breathing equipment; and pebbles, small smooth stones.

problem.en: Where was Shaana: (a) in a boat among mangroves; (b) rafting on a river that flows to the centre?

text.en: Recall the postcards.

why.en: Mangroves belong to the Sundarbans in West Bengal.

points.en: Shaana travels across India and writes postcards to her classmates.
She visits glaciers, mountains, wetlands, a desert, a river, plateaus and beaches.
Directions such as north, south, east and west tell us where places are.
The postcards show India's variety of landscapes, languages and people.
Postcards are written in an informal style.
